replies.text:
@gerardflynn3899 Scandinavia is a historical, cultural, and linguistic region rather than just a strictly geographical one. Since the mid-19th century, the term has specifically referred to the three kingdoms of Denmark, Norway, and Sweden, which share mutually intelligible North Germanic languages and deeply intertwined histories (such as the Kalmar Union).
While Denmark isn't located on the Scandinavian Peninsula (which is a purely geographical term for the landmass shared by Norway, Sweden, and northern Finland), it is still one of the three core countries that make up Scandinavia itself. In fact, the word "Scandinavia" originally referred to Scania (Skåne)—the southernmost tip of modern-day Sweden, which was historically part of Denmark for centuries!

@annabackman3028 
The term "Scandinavia" exists in various forms, the geographical definition being one of them. 
I am fully aware that there are only three Scandinavian countries, and that they share close linguistic, historical, and cultural ties. This does not preclude the existence of another interpretation of "Scandinavia"—in this case, referring to a part of Finland that offers a direct route through Sweden toward the south, should one wish to drive to the western part of the European continent. This is not to say that I do not respect the Finns' desire to define themselves as being outside of Scandinavia; however, I am from Northern Norway myself, and I have frequently driven through both Finland and Sweden to reach the southern parts of Norway.
